sec.title: Background
sec.p: Stepwise dual‐target MR‐guided Focused Ultrasound (dtMRgFUS) is a novel treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD), targeting both Ventral Intermediate Nucleus (VIM) and the pallidothalamic tract (PTT). While previous studies have demonstrated its 12‐month efficacy, this study focuses on the immediate effects of additional PTT lesioning after VIM ablation.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Twenty patients (age 69.3 ± 8.9 years) with both tremor and akinetic rigidity received dtMRgFUS when they were off medications, with a series of primary and secondary outcome measures on the table. We performed unilateral VIM first, with subsequent ipsilateral PTT ablation in the same session. The primary outcomes were the off‐status sub‐score of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale part III (UPDRS‐III) and the Clinical Rating Scale for Tremor (CRST). In addition, we compared the outcome changes from the baseline to the first VIM treatment with the changes from VIM treatment to the subsequent PTT treatment.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: During the procedure, the severity of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia improved significantly (all p < 0.05 by paired t‐test) after both VIM and PTT treatment. Notably, major improvement of parameters was noted after VIM lesioning (all p < 0.02 by paired t‐test), except for rigidity, which showed significant changes immediately after PTT lesioning (p < 0.02 by paired t‐test).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: These findings highlight the immediate therapeutic impact of PTT lesioning following VIM lesioning in the same treatment session, reinforcing its role as a crucial add‐on target for managing refractory PD symptoms beyond tremor. This dtMRgFUS approach offers a more comprehensive motor benefit, particularly for patients with rigidity.
Keywords: MR‐guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS), pallidothalamic tract, Parkinson's disease, stepwise dual‐target MRgFUS, thalamotomy, tremor, ventral intermediate nucleus

abstract.p: The PTT originates from the GPi and projects to the VA/VL thalamic nuclei via Forel's Fields, forming a key motor signal pathway. Lesioning the PTT may disrupt basal ganglia–thalamocortical circuits and related motor control. Connections through Forel's Fields also link the PTT to the PPN and subthalamic structures such as the ZI.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM) thalamotomy using Magnetic Resonance‐guided Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS) is a minimally invasive procedure aimed at treating tremors in Parkinson's disease (PD). This technique utilizes high‐intensity focused ultrasound waves to ablate brain tissue within the VIM, a crucial region implicated in tremor pathophysiology. Studies have demonstrated that MRgFUS thalamotomy effectively reduces both resting and postural/kinetic tremors, with significant improvements persisting for at least five years post‐treatment [1]. Remarkable tremor reduction in the treated hand is strongly correlated with functional reorganization in the motor and cerebellar regions [2]. The procedure is well‐tolerated, with most adverse effects being mild and transient. However, PD is a complex disease characterized not only by tremors but also by bradykinesia and rigidity. Abnormal oscillatory activity within the basal ganglia and inter‐circuit interactions, not just the cerebello‐thalamo‐cortical circuit, are also associated with PD symptoms [3]. The traditional MRgFUS targeting VIM may not satisfy the clinical needs for all tremor subtypes, nor address bradykinesia and rigidity [4, 5, 6, 7]. In our previous study, we reported a 12‐month follow‐up of 10 idiopathic PD patients who exhibited both tremor and akinetic‐rigid symptoms and received stepwise dual‐target MRgFUS (dtMRgFUS) with VIM and PTT lesioning in one treatment session in order to intervene in both the basal ganglia and cerebello‐thalamo‐cotical circuit [8]. Over a 12‐month follow‐up, the treated side showed sustained and significant improvement in CRST (A + B) scores, with benefits ranging from 75% to 83% (p < 0.001). Similarly, UPDRS‐III scores on the treated side, reflecting bradykinesia and rigidity, demonstrated consistent advancement, maintaining 70%–83% improvement throughout the year (p < 0.001). These findings suggest durable motor symptom relief, indicating the long‐term efficacy of the intervention. Additionally, no severe adverse effects were reported during the one‐year follow‐up [8]. However, the additive effect of PTT ablation was not yet clear due to the relatively small number of patients who initially received VIM‐first ablation.

In this study, we specifically evaluate the immediate impact of PTT lesioning as an add‐on target following VIM ablation in the same treatment session in PD patients with both tremor and akinetic‐rigid features. Data were collected from 20 patients who underwent neurological assessments directly on the treatment table to capture the real‐time effects of PTT lesioning. This approach aims to clarify the rapid motor benefits of PTT ablation and its role in optimizing dtMRgFUS for medication‐refractory PD symptoms.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: This case series enrolled 20 adult patients (> 20 year‐old) diagnosed with tremor‐dominant medication‐resistant Parkinson's disease (PD) who underwent MRgFUS treatment alongside standardized care. Basic data and symptom characteristics are shown in Table 1. The diagnosis of PD, as confirmed with the U.K. Brain Bank Clinical Criteria [9] from clinical history and examination, was made by neurologists specialized in movement disorders at a tertiary medical center, China Medical University Hospital, Taiwan. An inadequate medication response was defined as the failure to achieve satisfactory symptom control despite receiving therapeutic doses of antiparkinsonian medications. This was determined by one or more of the following criteria: (1) a lack of meaningful clinical response to appropriately titrated doses, indicating medication resistance; (2) suboptimal drug efficacy, where improvements were insufficient to maintain functional independence or quality of life; or (3) the emergence of intolerable side effects, such as dyskinesia, orthostatic hypotension, cognitive impairment, or gastrointestinal disturbances, that limited further dose escalation. Patients meeting any of these criteria were considered candidates for MR‐guided focused ultrasound. The analysis of the on‐table examination results included five patients whose one‐year follow‐up data had been previously published [6].

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: All patients included in this analysis provided written informed consent after receiving comprehensive information about the treatment. They also granted permission for the publication of their anonymized data. The study adhered to the standards set by the Declaration of Helsinki and received approval from the China Medical University Hospital in Taiwan (CMUH111‐REC3‐014).

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: The procedure and data collection of MRgFUS was described as our previous study [8]. VIM was targeted first, followed by PTT lesioning. Clinical outcomes of one‐day, 6‐month follow‐up, and on‐table measurements were reported here, including the off‐status CRST and UPDRS part III. Secondary outcome measures consisted of UPDRS part I, II, IV, and Hoehn and Yahr score (HY). The patients were off Parkinson's medication for at least 12 h. On‐table parameters were collected during the procedure while the patients were in the “off” medication state. Resting tremor, action tremor, and postural tremor were evaluated using the CRST. Rigidity and finger tapping were assessed using the UPDRS. Baseline data were collected before the localizing sonications started. The clinical assessments of patients were conducted by a specialized movement disorder nurse, who independently graded the scores in a blinded manner to ensure objective evaluation. To minimize the carry‐over effect—where clinical improvements following PTT lesioning may in fact result from transient edema induced by prior VIM sonications—the final VIM effect scores were recorded immediately before the first effective PTT lesioning. Although a VIM examination was conducted after the initial suprathreshold VIM sonication, this post‐sonication evaluation was not used for final VIM effect scoring. The PTT effect scores were then recorded immediately after the first effective PTT lesioning, defined as reaching a suprathreshold temperature exceeding 50°C (Figure 1). Although most clinical protocols typically target higher temperatures, previous literature has shown that temperatures exceeding 50°C can induce protein denaturation and cell necrosis [3]. Based on our experience, a temperature of 50°C sustained for a prolonged duration was sufficient to produce a definitive lesion. In the majority of patients, we achieved temperatures exceeding 55°C. In a few cases with low skull density ratios, achieving higher temperatures was particularly challenging, but with a temperature > 50°C, the permanent treatment effect was achieved for more than 6 months.

caption.p: Intraoperative workflow of stepwise dual‐target MRgFUS treatment. The procedure follows a structured sequence beginning with baseline clinical examination, followed by stepwise sonication of the VIM and PTT targets. Subthreshold and suprathreshold sonications are applied to confirm target localization and therapeutic effect. Clinical assessments were performed after each major lesioning step. Highlighted boxes indicate key evaluation points: Baseline examination, VIM effect examination, and PTT effect examination.

sec.p: To evaluate potential off‐target effects of PTT lesioning, we analyzed post‐treatment one‐day 3D T1‐weighted MR images. The intended PTT target was defined as the midpoint along the anterior commissure–posterior commissure (AC‐PC) line, with a lateral displacement of 4–10 mm from the medial wall of the third ventricle. The actual lesion location was then measured in relation to this predefined target.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Repeated Measures ANOVA (rmANOVA) was applied to analyze the differences across multiple stages (Baseline, VIM, PTT) for Clinical Scores on the Treatment Table. Post hoc tests were used to identify which specific pairs of treatments (Baseline vs. VIM, VIM vs. PTT, and Baseline vs. PTT) exhibited significant differences after a significant result was found in rmANOVA with Bonferroni correction. Paired t‐test was used to examine the mean scores for One‐day Follow‐up and mean changes between “Baseline to VIM” and “VIM to PTT” for the on‐table exam. Mean values are presented with their corresponding standard deviations. Significance was determined by a p value below 0.05.

sec.title: One‐Day and 6‐Month Follow‐Up
sec.p: In this study, 20 idiopathic PD patients presenting both resting and postural/kinetic tremors (aged 69.3 ± 8.9 years, 17 men) were included. Twelve participants had dominant symptoms on the right side. A total of 20 subjects were successfully treated, and the on‐table examination and 1‐day follow‐up were completed. Fourteen participants also completed the 6‐month follow‐up, while six were lost to follow‐up, primarily owing to travel distance. As the primary aim of this study was to report on immediate treatment outcomes, early post‐treatment data were prioritized. Paired t‐test analyses demonstrated significant improvements across multiple clinical parameters after treatment. The UPDRS Part III (treated side) score improved from 13.6 ± 4.1 at baseline to 2.1 ± 1.6 at 1 day post‐treatment (t(19) = 12.9, p < 0.00), and to 2.4 ± 2.4 at 6 months (t(13) = 9.1, p < 0.00). Additional significant improvements were noted in UPDRS Part III, rigidity, bradykinesia, and tremor subscores, with sustained effects observed at 6 months post‐treatment. These results support the efficacy of the intervention in producing rapid and durable motor symptom relief. Detailed results are presented in Table 1.

LEDD (Levodopa‐Equivalent Daily Dose) showed a non‐significant change from baseline to 1 day post‐treatment, with mean values of 617 ± 337 mg at baseline and 611 ± 333 mg at 1 day (t(16) = 0.99, p = 0.34, n = 17). However, a significant reduction was observed at 6 months, with LEDD decreasing from 596 ± 363 mg to 446 ± 344 mg (t(10) = 2.84, p = 0.02, n = 11). This suggests that although the immediate change in LEDD was minimal, long‐term dose reduction may be achievable following treatment. It might also be noted that 3 patients did not receive any medications before or after treatment due to medication side effects.

sec.title: Clinical Scores on the Treatment Table
sec.p: The clinical scores on the table revealed the following mean (± standard deviation) scores for each parameter across the Baseline, VIM, and PTT stages with 95% confidence intervals (Figure 2): Resting Tremor (Baseline: 5.2 ± 2.19, 95% CI [4.17, 6.23]; VIM: 1.9 ± 2.02, 95% CI [0.95, 2.85]; PTT: 0.5 ± 1.19, 95% CI [−0.06, 1.06]), Posture Tremor (Baseline: 3.1 ± 0.79, 95% CI [2.73, 3.47]; VIM: 1.2 ± 0.62, 95% CI [0.91, 1.49]; PTT: 0.4 ± 0.50, 95% CI [0.16, 0.64]), Action Tremor (Baseline: 3.1 ± 0.79, 95% CI [2.73, 3.47]; VIM: 1.15 ± 0.67, 95% CI [0.84, 1.46]; PTT: 0.25 ± 0.44, 95% CI [0.04, 0.46]), Rigidity (Baseline: 2.5 ± 1.70, 95% CI [1.70, 3.30]; VIM: 1.8 ± 1.20, 95% CI [1.24, 2.36]; PTT: 0.3 ± 0.66, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.61]), and Finger Taps (Baseline: 2.55 ± 1.05, 95% CI [2.06, 3.04]; VIM: 1.1 ± 0.72, 95% CI [0.76, 1.44]; PTT: 0.3 ± 0.57, 95% CI [0.03, 0.57]).

caption.p: The clinical scores of baseline, VIM and PTT during MRgFUS. Significant differences were noted in each parameter. Tremor scores were based on CRST, part A (contains tremor at rest (upper and lower extremities), posture and action), while rigidity (upper and lower extremities) and finger taps were based on UPDRS Part III. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01 by t‐test compared between conditions.

sec.p: Repeated Measures ANOVA (rmANOVA) confirmed significant differences across the stages for all parameters: Resting Tremor (F(2,38) = 70.18, p < 0.00), Posture Tremor (F(2,38) = 117.88, p < 0.001), Action Tremor (F(2,38) = 145.32, p < 0.00), Rigidity (F(2,38) = 34.96, p < 0.00), and Finger Taps (F(2,38) = 87.49, p < 0.00). Post hoc analysis with Bonferroni correction indicated significant reductions in scores from Baseline to VIM, Baseline to PTT, and VIM to PTT for all parameters (p < 0.05) (Figure 2).

These findings suggest that VIM significantly improves tremor, rigidity, and finger taps. Further improvements from VIM to PTT were also remarkable, highlighting the effectiveness of both targets and the add‐on effect of PTT after VIM lesioning.

sec.title: Mean Changes Between “Baseline to VIM” and “VIM to PTT”
sec.p: The mean changes between “Baseline to VIM” and “VIM to PTT” revealed significant differences across all clinical parameters (Figure 3 and Table 2). For resting Tremor, the mean change from Baseline to VIM was 3.30 ± 1.72 (95% CI [2.50, 4.10]), and from VIM to PTT was 1.40 ± 1.54 (95% CI [0.68, 2.12]), with a significant p value < 0.00. Posture Tremor showed a mean change of 1.90 ± 0.64 (95% CI [1.60, 2.20]) from Baseline to VIM, and 0.80 ± 0.70 (95% CI [0.47, 1.13]) from VIM to PTT, with a p value < 0.00. Action Tremor had mean changes of 1.95 ± 0.69 (95% CI [1.63, 2.27]) and 0.90 ± 0.72 (95% CI [0.56, 1.24]), respectively, with a p value < 0.00. Finger Taps improved significantly, with mean changes of 1.45 ± 0.83 (95% CI [1.06, 1.84]) from Baseline to VIM, and 0.80 ± 0.62 (95% CI [0.51, 1.09]) from VIM to PTT, with a p value < 0.02. For Rigidity, the trend was different; the mean change from Baseline to VIM was 0.70 ± 1.03 (95% CI [0.22, 1.18]), while from VIM to PTT was significantly larger at 1.50 ± 1.00 (95% CI [1.03, 1.97]), with a p value < 0.02. These results highlight the majority of improvements after VIM were tremors and bradykinesia, while rigidity improved notably after PTT lesioning.

The findings indicate that the most significant improvements following VIM treatment were seen in tremor and bradykinesia, while PTT treatment particularly led to a marked improvement in rigidity. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01 by t‐test compared between conditions.

sec.title: Off‐Target Assessment of PTT Lesion
sec.p: Across all 20 subjects, the mean lesion was located 0.03 ± 0.60 mm inferior to the AC‐PC plane, 0.15 ± 0.74 mm anterior to the midpoint of the AC‐PC line, and 8.41 ± 1.06 mm lateral to the third ventricle wall according to the 24 h post‐treatment imaging (Figure 4).

caption.p: Lesion analysis of PTT target. The white spheres show the PTT lesions of all 20 subjects in standard axial and coronal images. The lesion placement was highly consistent with the planned target zone, minimizing the likelihood of off‐target effects. A, anterior; GP, globus pallidus; I, inferior; IC, internal capsule; L, left; R, right; S, superior; SN, substantia nigra; STN, subthalamic nucleus; Th, thalamus.

sec.title: Adverse Events
sec.p: Patients reported temporary headache, pain, and dizziness during treatment, which resolved by follow‐up assessments. Mild tilting toward the treated side was observed in four patients at 1‐day follow‐up, with none persisting at the 6‐month follow‐up. At one‐day post‐treatment, five patients experienced mild salivation; among them, three also had mild dysphagia and reported mild speech disturbances, primarily hypophonia. By the 6‐month follow‐up, only two patients continued to have mild salivation, with no remaining dysphagia or speech disturbance. No other significant adverse events, including weakness, numbness, or dyskinesia, occurred during treatment or within the first day and 6‐month post‐treatment. A comprehensive overview of these adverse events is provided in Table 3.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We observed a clear and immediate additive effect of PTT ablation following VIM ablation in reducing tremor and akinetic‐rigid symptoms in 20 PD patients undergoing dtMRgFUS. While tremor and bradykinesia improved significantly after VIM ablation, rigidity showed substantial and immediate relief following add‐on PTT lesioning. In our previous study, we demonstrated the 12‐month benefits of stepwise dtMRgFUS in addressing all tremor subtypes and akinetic‐rigid symptoms in a single treatment. Here, we further clarify the immediate therapeutic advantage of integrating PTT ablation with VIM targeting (Table 2). In conclusion, PTT ablation immediately enhances the overall efficacy of MRgFUS treatment, particularly in relieving rigidity, reinforcing its role as a critical add‐on target for comprehensive PD symptom management.

MRgFUS is a promising treatment for PD, particularly for patients with medication‐resistant tremors, offering significant symptom relief with a relatively favorable safety profile. The systematic review by Xu et al. (2021) evaluates the safety and efficacy of MRgFUS for treating medication‐resistant Parkinson's disease (PD) [10]. This review includes data from 11 studies, encompassing 80 patients, primarily focusing on tremor‐dominant PD. The review indicates significant motor symptom improvement in most cases, with 10 studies reporting a reduction in UPDRS‐III scores, and five studies showing statistically significant improvement. Notably, tremor reduction was consistently observed, with some studies reporting an improvement in UPDRS‐III scores from baseline to follow‐up, for example, from 23.0 to 14.5 at 3 months and 13.0 at 12 months in Bond et al.'s study [11]. The systematic review suggests that MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy is effective for managing tremor in tremor‐dominant PD. However, the VIM appears to have limited relevance to other primary symptoms of PD, such as rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural disturbances, in line with VIM deep brain stimulation (DBS), which does not significantly alleviate these symptoms either [12].

In our previous paper, we proposed in addition to VIM, add‐on PTT lesion in one treatment course could alleviate the cardinal symptoms of PD, including rigidity and bradykinesia [8]. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of dual‐target MRgFUS for treating medication‐resistant tremor and akinetic‐rigid features in ten patients (mean age 66.7 ± 3.2 years). Outcome measures were assessed at baseline and follow‐up points (1 day, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year). Significant improvements were observed in tremor (75%–83%) and akinetic/rigid syndromes (70%–83%) as measured by CRST‐part A + B and UPDRS III scores. Non‐motor symptoms and quality of life also improved, with no severe adverse effects reported. The findings suggest that stepwise dtMRgFUS is a safe and effective treatment modality for addressing medication‐refractory tremor and akinetic‐rigid syndrome in PD patients.

With a larger patient cohort, this study further clarifies the immediate additive benefits of PTT lesioning. Consistent with our previous findings, stepwise dtMRgFUS significantly improved UPDRS Part III scores. Clinical assessments revealed rapid improvements in resting tremor, postural tremor, action tremor, rigidity, and finger‐tap performance at both steps: from Baseline to VIM and from VIM to PTT. While tremor and finger‐tap function improved immediately after VIM lesioning, rigidity showed the most pronounced and immediate relief following PTT ablation, underscoring its crucial role in alleviating muscle stiffness. Paired t‐tests confirmed statistically significant differences across all measures, reinforcing the real‐time efficacy of PTT in optimizing MRgFUS outcomes. These findings suggest PTT lesioning as an essential add‐on target, particularly for rigidity, enhancing the overall therapeutic impact of dtMRgFUS in PD patients. Meanwhile, it was worth noting that none of our patients who underwent dtMRgFUS developed dyskinesia after the ablations. This result brings strong advantages against ablations at other targets.

PTT is composed of two distinct fiber bundles: the ansa lenticularis and the lenticular fasciculus (Figure 5). These bundles connect the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) to thalamic subnuclei, such as the ventral anterior nucleus and the ventrolateral nucleus [13]. Originating from different parts of the GPi, the bundles travel across the internal capsule and converge at the field of Forel, where they unite to form a single fiber known as the “thalamic fasciculus” [14]. Horisawa et al. prospectively evaluated the efficacy and safety of thermal ablation by radiofrequency on unilateral PTT for asymmetric rigid Parkinson's disease (AR‐PD). One year post‐surgery, patients exhibited a 50% improvement in clinician‐scored motor evaluations, including contralateral rigidity and bradykinesia.

caption.p: The PTT consists of the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus, originating from the internal segment of the GPi and projecting to the VA and VL thalamic nuclei. These fiber bundles converge at Forel's Fields (H1 and H2) to form the thalamic fasciculus, a critical motor signal pathway. The PPN, located in the upper pons and lower midbrain, also connects with the basal ganglion via the connections through Forel's Fields (H1 and H2). ZI is a small gray matter region in the subthalamus area. Our lesion of PTT may disrupt motor control through these connections. GPi, globus pallidus internus; IC, internal capsule; MTT, mammillothalamic tract; PPN, pedunculopontine nucleus; PTT, pedunculopontine tract; SN, substantia nigra; STN, subthalamic nucleus; VA, ventral anterior nucleus; VIM, ventral intermediate nucleus; VL, ventrolateral nucleus; ZI, zona incerta.

sec.p: The PTT plays a critical role in addressing motor dysfunction in PD by targeting excessive inhibition from the GPi. In PD, dopaminergic neuron loss disrupts the basal ganglia–thalamocortical loop, causing GPi hyperactivity. This leads to over‐inhibition of the thalamus, impairing motor signal transmission to the cortex and contributing to symptoms like rigidity, bradykinesia, and tremor [15, 16]. PTT lesioning reduces this overactive GPi inhibition, restoring thalamic and cortical motor signal flow and alleviating rigidity.

The zona incerta (ZI) is also underlying within our target (Figure 5). Being a small gray matter region in the subthalamus, ZI plays a critical modulatory role in motor control through its extensive connections involved in PD pathology. The ZI has become an important target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) while it effectively alleviates parkinsonian symptoms such as bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, and tremor. The therapeutic effects of ZI DBS are thought to arise from its ability to disrupt abnormal information flow, including pallidothalamic and cerebellothalamic pathways. While the full scope of its functions remains unclear, the ZI's extensive interactions with the basal ganglia, thalamus, and dopaminergic systems underscore its importance in motor regulation and its therapeutic potential for managing movement disorders like PD [17].

The pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), located in the upper pons and lower midbrain, may also play a role in regulating muscle tone regarding PTT lesioning. Composed of cholinergic (PPNc), glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurons (PPNd), the PPN integrates motor signals through connections with the basal ganglia, thalamus, and spinal cord [18]. GPi hyperactivity disrupts PPN function in PD via the connections through Forel's Fields (H1 and H2). By lesioning the PTT, the restored balance of motor inputs via the PPN and thalamus enhances motor signal coordination with the cortex, providing relief from rigidity [19].

The present study has limitations. First, the carry‐over effect, that is, the effectiveness of PTT lesioning being induced by transient edema due to previous sonications, has been a concern. Trying to avoid that, we measured the clinical score immediately before and after the first effective PTT lesioning. Latency of less than 10 min between the two measurements was noted, which might minimize the carry‐over effect. However, the subthreshold effect of PTT alignments still needs to be taken into consideration in the data interpretation. Although STN was not our intended target, the proximity of the PTT to the STN makes minor involvement of the STN unavoidable in some patients. Conducting a double‐blinded, randomized control trial with VIM‐only as the control group could mitigate this bias more effectively. Second, the long‐term effect of add‐on PTT is not yet clear. Therefore, long‐term follow‐up and evaluations are mandatory.

This study highlights the immediate additive effect of PTT lesioning following VIM ablation in treating the cardinal motor symptoms of PD. Significant and rapid reductions in tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia were observed, with rigidity showing the most notable immediate relief after PTT lesioning. No serious adverse effects were reported. These findings emphasize the critical role of PTT as an add‐on target, reinforcing its potential to enhance the efficacy of MRgFUS in patients with refractory PD symptoms. Given its immediate therapeutic impact on rigidity, PTT lesioning should be integrated into treatment consideration, particularly for addressing rigidity, to optimize patient outcomes.
